title: Scheduler-batching timeout & fairness experiment log
content:
Purpose:
This is an experiment log capturing a set of controlled runs to understand how scheduler knobs (max_batch_size, batch_timeout_ms, fairness scheduling) interact with tail latency and throughput for realistic mixed workloads. The goal is actionable guidance for default config and a short list of mitigation changes (code + config) to reduce p95/p99 regressions without sacrificing too much throughput.

High-level hypotheses (what we wanted to test):
- H1: Increasing max_batch_size improves overall throughput but increases p99 for short requests (<=32 tokens) due to batching-induced queuing.
- H2: Aggressive timeouts (low batch_timeout_ms) reduce tail latency for small requests but hurt GPU utilization and throughput for long requests.
- H3: A fairness-aware scheduler (priority by token-estimate or request-size) reduces starvation of small requests and reduces p99 while keeping throughput within 5% of baseline.

Test harness and workload setup:
- Cluster: 4 machines, each 8xA100 80GB, same CUDA/cuDNN driver, isolated from other experiments.
- Runtime: serving-runtime v0.38.1 (branch: batching-experiments) with lightweight tracing enabled.
- Workload generator: custom harness that replays production-ish mix from last 7 days sampling: 70% short requests (<=32 tokens), 20% medium (33-256 tokens), 10% long (>256 tokens). QPS scaled so baseline GPU utilization ~75%.
- Measurement windows: 15 minute warmup, 60 minute measurement. Collected metrics: requests/sec, tokens/sec, p50/p90/p95/p99 latency (inference queue + model time), batching stats (avg batch size, batch count, batch wait time), scheduler queue depth, CPU-side lock contention metrics (mutex hold time), and nvprof summaries for kernel launch/hto/dto overhead.

Config matrix (representative subset):
- A: max_batch_size=64, batch_timeout_ms=10, fairness=off (baseline)
- B: max_batch_size=128, batch_timeout_ms=20, fairness=off
- C: max_batch_size=64, batch_timeout_ms=2, fairness=off
- D: max_batch_size=64, batch_timeout_ms=10, fairness=per-request-size (small-first)
- E: max_batch_size=32, batch_timeout_ms=5, fairness=off
- F: max_batch_size=128, batch_timeout_ms=5, fairness=per-token-priority

Quick summary of results (aggregated across 4 machines):
- Baseline A: throughput 100k tokens/sec, p99 latency 220ms, avg batch size 48 for mixed workload.
- B (larger batches): throughput +18% vs A, p99 +42% (to 313ms), avg batch size 96. Tail increases mostly for small requests.
- C (low timeout): throughput -9% vs A, p99 -36% (to 141ms), avg batch size 30. Lower GPU efficiency observed from smaller batches.
- D (fairness small-first): throughput -3% vs A, p99 -18% (to 181ms), avg batch size 46 for medium/long, but small requests median latency improved by ~55ms.
- E (small max batch): throughput -23% vs A, p99 -28% (to 159ms), GPU utilization dropped significantly; not acceptable for high-cost customers.
- F (large batch + token priority): throughput +10% vs A, p99 -5% vs A (210ms), but observed jitter in p95 where medium requests sometimes got delayed.

Profiling and root-cause notes (hotspots discovered):
- Queue contention: kernel-level tracing showed spikes in mutex contention inside the scheduler's global queue when batch arrival rate fluctuates. Contention contributes ~8-12ms average wait at p99.
- Wakeup bursts: When batch_timeout_ms expires, many request handler threads wake and contend; this causes CPU-side scheduling jitter and occasional 10-30ms variance in batching start times.
- Small-request starvation: With larger max_batch_size, small requests often sit behind accumulating large requests; fairness policies that estimate token count at enqueue time mitigate but add scheduling overhead.
- CUDA overhead: For small batches, the per-call kernel launch and H2D latency become dominant; nvprof shows kernel launch overhead ~1.8ms per call and H2D copies proportionally higher under smaller batch counts.
- Serialization costs: Tokenization + JSON marshalling on the CPU path added 5-12ms for small requests. Offloading tokenization or batching tokenization tasks reduces variance.

Observations and trade-offs:
- Low timeout is effective at reducing p99 for small requests but costs throughput; acceptable for latency-sensitive customers but not for throughput-optimized tiers.
- Fairness policies (size-based priority) hit a sweet spot: small throughput loss (~3-5%) but meaningful p99 improvements without drastic throughput drop. Complexity increases (need accurate token estimate at enqueue).
- Adaptive hybrid: start with larger max_batch_size but dynamically reduce batch_timeout_ms when short-request fraction rises above threshold; this approach improved p99 by ~15% while only reducing throughput 6% in experiments.

Detailed numbers (selected):
- Config A: avg_batch_size=48, avg_batch_wait_ms=9.8, p99=220ms, throughput=100k toks/s
- Config B: avg_batch_size=96, avg_batch_wait_ms=18.4, p99=313ms, throughput=118k toks/s
- Config D: avg_batch_size_small=6, avg_batch_size_medium=42, avg_batch_wait_ms_small=3.1, p99=181ms, throughput=97k toks/s

Immediate recommendations for defaults:
1) For hosted API tier: enable fairness=per-request-size by default with max_batch_size=96 and default batch_timeout_ms=10, but use adaptive timeout that reduces to 5ms when short-request ratio >60%. Rationale: keeps throughput high while protecting p99 for the majority of users.
2) For dedicated/throughput-optimized: expose batch_timeout_ms knob to customers and document expected p99/throughput tradeoffs; default to max_batch_size=128, timeout=20ms.
3) Add a sampling profiler to capture mutex hold time and wakeup spikes in production for 1% of traffic (lightweight).

Code-level follow-ups and engineering TODOs:
- Reduce scheduler global lock scope: convert global queue to sharded queues by CPU core to reduce contention spikes (SRV-541).
- Implement lightweight token-size estimator at enqueue time to avoid full tokenization (prototype exists in branch "quick-estimator").
- Add jittered wakeup stamping to spread batch timeouts by a few hundred microseconds to avoid thundering-wakeup.
- Expose internal metrics: avg_batch_wait_ms broken out by request-size bucket.
- Experiment with a cooperative small-request fast-path that bypasses batching for sub-20-token requests when queue depth below threshold.

Open questions / next experiments:
- What is impact of sharded queues on memory usage and complexity (latency regressions for long requests)?
- Can we implement adaptive batching that uses ML (lightweight) to pick timeout per GPU based on recent mix? Is the operational complexity worth it?
- Measure impact of moving tokenization off CPU main thread onto a worker pool shared across processes.

Notes to reviewers:
- Raw CSVs and nvprof outputs uploaded to: https://internal-redwood-storage/experiments/batching/2025-01-12-runs (request access via SRV-ops).
- See PR https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/812 for the fairness scheduler prototype.
- Linear tickets: SRV-482 (regression investigation), SRV-541 (sharded-queue refactor).

Quick TODO (priority ordering):
- [P0] Add sharded queue prototype and run 1 cluster-level A/B test (owner: Evan)
- [P1] Merge token-size estimator and run low-cost trial on 10% traffic (owner: Priya)
- [P2] Add sampling profiler metric and Grafana dashboard for batch-wait-ms by size (owner: Lila)

Appendix (observational notes):
- During a rainy-day traffic pattern (burst with 3x short-request fraction), configs with fixed large batch sizes saw p99 blowouts to >500ms; adaptive timeouts performed best in that scenario.
- Customers on dedicated plans explicitly demanded throughput-first configs; recommend adding presets in Console: "latency-sensitive" vs "throughput-optimized".

End of log.
